status: drafted via lean single-pass workflow grounded in the real extracted verse text
notes: Read the full Ethiopian-translation text (14 chapters, 197 verses) directly from hosea_48.json. Content and wording are essentially identical to the KJV Hosea already indexed at CharacterIndex/Hosea.json (verse-for-verse match on every checked passage: 1:2-11 sign-children, 2:1-23 restoration oracle, 3:1-5 buy-back, 6:6 mercy-not-sacrifice, 11:1 Egypt/son, 12:3-4/12 Jacob allusions, 14:1-9 closing call to return) — no real Ethiopian-specific textual divergence was found in this book, unlike the Ezra case. Adapted the KJV structure's proven tier shape (2 person tiers + 5 law/theme tiers + 3 sign-named submanagers) rather than inventing a new one, but re-verified every verse reference, quote, and genealogy note directly against this translation's own extracted text before including it. All character/law ids suffixed '_ethiopian' to avoid collision with the existing KJV Hosea ids. Naming-collision flag carried over and re-confirmed in this text: the prophet Hosea (1:1, 'son of Beeri') shares his underlying Hebrew name with Hoshea the last king of Israel and with Oshea/Joshua's original name, and the 'Jeroboam' of the 1:1 superscription is Jeroboam II son of Joash (Israel's contemporary king), not Jeroboam I son of Nebat who founded the calf worship condemned later in the book (8:5-6, 10:5) — only the patronymic 'son of Joash' in 1:1 disambiguates this, so it is flagged explicitly rather than left implicit. The unnamed prophet of 12:13 ('by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt') is traditionally understood as Moses but is not named in this text, so no character entry was created for that reference beyond a note in the Israel's Sinful History law tier. Gomer's identification with the unnamed woman of 3:1 ('a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress') is traditional, not textually confirmed in chapter 3 itself, and is flagged as such rather than asserted as fact. characters.name: Hosea

genealogy.note: Identified only as 'the son of Beeri' (1:1); no mother named. Ministry dated to the reigns of Judah's kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, and Israel's king Jeroboam the son of Joash (Jeroboam II) — not to be confused with the earlier Jeroboam I son of Nebat, founder of the calf worship condemned at 8:5-6 and 10:5.

verses.note: Superscription: 'the word of the LORD that came unto Hosea, the son of Beeri' — dates his ministry by the kings of Judah and Israel.
Commanded, 'Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms'; he takes Gomer the daughter of Diblaim.
Commanded again to love an adulterous woman; buys her back 'for fifteen pieces of silver, and for an homer of barley, and an half homer of barley.'
Tells her she must abide with him many days without playing the harlot — a picture of Israel's coming discipline before restoration.

funFacts: His name means 'salvation,' sharing its root with Joshua and Jesus.
The prophet 'Hosea' shares his underlying Hebrew name with 'Hoshea,' the last king of Israel (2 Kings 17:1), and with 'Oshea,' Joshua's original name (Numbers 13:16) — three different people.
The only Old Testament prophet whose own marriage is used as a sustained, multi-chapter living parable of God's relationship to Israel.

characters.name: Gomer

genealogy.note: Called 'the daughter of Diblaim' (1:3). The unnamed woman Hosea is commanded to love again in 3:1 ('a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress') is traditionally identified with Gomer, but chapter 3 does not name her again — this text does not itself confirm the identification.

verses.note: 'So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim which conceived, and bare him a son.'
Pursues 'lovers,' crediting them for bread, water, wool, flax, oil, and drink.
'she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil' — the LORD, not Baal, was the true source.
Restoration oracle: the LORD betroths Israel to himself forever 'in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies.'

funFacts: Bears three children whose divinely-given names function as prophetic sign-acts against Israel.
In chapter 2 the LORD addresses 'your mother' (Israel personified through Gomer) as having credited Baal for grain, wine, and oil that were actually His gifts (2:5, 8).

characters.name: Jezreel

genealogy.note: Firstborn son; named directly by the LORD's command, not chosen by his parents (1:4).

verses.note: 'Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu... and I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.'
'great shall be the day of Jezreel' — his name reused as a title of future restoration.
'they shall hear Jezreel. And I will sow her unto me in the earth' — wordplay on his name (God sows/scatters).

funFacts: Name means 'God sows' or 'God scatters'; also the valley/city where Jehu massacred the house of Ahab and where Ahab seized Naboth's vineyard.
His name's meaning is reversed from judgment to hope by the book's end.

characters.name: Lo-ruhamah

genealogy.note: Daughter; named 'Lo-ruhamah' ('not pitied'/'not having obtained mercy') by direct divine command (1:6).

verses.note: 'Call her name Lo-ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel but I will utterly take them away.'
By contrast, the LORD says He 'will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and will save them by the LORD their God' at this same time.
'Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi and to your sisters, Ru-hamah' — the reversal.
'I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy.'

funFacts: Her name is reversed in the restoration oracle to 'Ruhamah' (mercy obtained).
Marks the point where God withholds mercy from Israel specifically while showing mercy to Judah at the same time (1:6-7).

characters.name: Lo-ammi

genealogy.note: Second son; named 'Lo-ammi' ('not my people') by direct divine command (1:9).

verses.note: 'Call his name Lo-ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.'
Immediately followed by a promise Israel's number will be 'as the sand of the sea' and they will be called 'the sons of the living God.'
'I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people and they shall say, Thou art my God.'

funFacts: His name is reversed to 'Ammi' ('my people') in the restoration oracle.
1:10's promise, paired with his harsh naming, is quoted by Paul in Romans 9:25-26.

characters.name: Baal Worship
characters.purpose: Frames Israel's idolatry as marital infidelity — Israel credits Baal for the corn, wine, oil, wool, and flax the LORD actually provided (2:8-9), pursues Baal under shady trees on the hills (4:13), and must be stripped bare and led back into the wilderness to be won again (2:3-15).

verses.note: Israel did not know the LORD gave the corn, wine, and oil later 'prepared for Baal.'
'the days of Baalim, wherein she burned incense to them' — judged, along with her earrings and jewels worn for her lovers.
Restoration: Israel will call the LORD 'Ishi' (my husband), no longer 'Baali'; the names of Baalim taken away out of her mouth.
Sacrifices offered 'upon the tops of the mountains... under oaks and poplars and elms, because the shadow thereof is good.'
Recalls Israel going 'to Baal-peor, and separated themselves unto that shame.'
'they sacrificed unto Baalim, and burned incense to graven images.'
'when he offended in Baal, he died' — Ephraim's fall tied directly to Baal worship.

funFacts: The Hebrew word 'baal' also simply means 'husband/lord' — part of the book's wordplay (2:16-17).
The LORD vows to 'take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth... they shall no more be remembered by their name' (2:17).

characters.name: Calf Worship
characters.purpose: Condemns Israel's self-manufactured golden-calf worship as illegitimate, homegrown idolatry distinct from Baal worship — 'the workman made it: therefore it is not God' (8:6) — doomed to be broken in pieces and carried off as tribute to Assyria (10:6).

verses.note: 'Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast thee off... the workman made it, therefore it is not God: but the calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces.'
'The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear because of the calves of Beth-aven.'
The calf-idol 'shall be also carried unto Assyria for a present to king Jareb.'
'they have made them molten images of their silver, and idols... Let the men that sacrifice kiss the calves.'

funFacts: This text does not name the calves' original royal sponsor; 1 Kings 12:28-29 credits Jeroboam I's shrines at Bethel and Dan.
10:6 pictures the calf-idol itself carried off to Assyria as tribute — the object of worship becomes a captive.

characters.name: Israel's Sinful History Recalled
characters.purpose: Argues Israel's present unfaithfulness continues a long pattern of rebellion — reaching back to the patriarch Jacob, the days at Gibeah, and the Exodus from Egypt itself — and of foolish alliance-seeking with Egypt and Assyria instead of trust in the LORD.

verses.note: 'they like men have transgressed the covenant: there have they dealt treacherously against me' — a broken covenant recalled.
'Ephraim is a cake not turned' — half-baked, ruined by mixing with foreign peoples.
Ephraim 'like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria.'
'they have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah.'
Israel's shame at 'Baal-peor' in the wilderness recalled.
'O Israel, thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah' repeated.
'When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.'
Recalls Jacob taking 'his brother by the heel in the womb' and having 'power with God... over the angel, and prevailed.'
Recalls Jacob fleeing 'into the country of Syria' and serving for a wife, keeping sheep.
'by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet was he preserved' — the prophet is not named in this text (traditionally understood as Moses).

funFacts: Hosea 11:1 is quoted by Matthew (2:15) of the infant Jesus' return from Egypt.
Hosea 7:11 compares Ephraim to 'a silly dove without heart' flitting between Egypt and Assyria for help instead of the LORD.

characters.name: Mercy, Not Sacrifice
characters.purpose: Declares that steadfast covenant love ('mercy') and relational knowledge of God matter more to the LORD than ritual sacrifice — one of the book's central theological statements, among the most quoted verses in the Minor Prophets.

verses.note: 'there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in the land.'
'My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee.'
'For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.' Quoted by Jesus in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7.

funFacts: Sits just after the LORD's complaint that 'your goodness is as a morning cloud, and as the early dew it goeth away' (6:4), immediately before this explanation of what He truly desires.

characters.name: Call to Return
characters.purpose: Invites Israel to abandon idols and return to the LORD in genuine repentance, promising healing, free love, and flourishing restoration — the book's closing resolution to the marriage/harlotry metaphor developed throughout.

verses.note: 'Come, and let us return unto the LORD: for he hath torn, and he will heal us he hath smitten, and he will bind us up.'
'O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God... Take with you words, and turn to the LORD... so will we render the calves of our lips.'
'I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him.'
'I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon.'
Closing wisdom saying: 'the ways of the LORD are right, and the just shall walk in them: but the transgressors shall fall therein.'

funFacts: 14:2 has Israel offer 'the calves of our lips' (praise) instead of animal sacrifice when returning to the LORD.
14:8 has the LORD say 'I am like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found' — reversing the false 'green tree' idolatry condemned at 4:13.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk/unresolved references kept out of the character list.

jacob_allusion.note: Historical recollection of Jacob's Genesis narrative (heel-grasping at birth, wrestling the angel, fleeing to Syria, serving for a wife) — already fully indexed as a character under Genesis; not re-indexed here since he takes no independent action within Hosea itself.
